title: Rangappa vs Sri Mohan
facts: The appellant-accused is a mechanic who engaged the services of the respondent-complainant, a Civil Engineer, for constructing his house in Ranebennur. The construction was completed on 20-10-1998.

As per the complainant, in October 1998, the accused requested a hand loan of Rs. 45,000 for construction expenses, which was paid in cash. The accused initially assured repayment by October 1999 but later sought more time until December 2000.
The accused issued a post-dated cheque for 8-2-2001 for Rs. 45,000. When presented, the bank returned the cheque with the memo stating 'Payment has been stopped by the drawer'.
The accused's first defense was that the cheque in question was a blank signed cheque which he had lost, and that it had come into the hands of the complainant who then misused it.
issues: Proper interpretation of Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, which shifts the burden of proof onto the accused in cheque bouncing cases.
Clarification on the manner in which the statutory presumption can be rebutted.
analysis_of_law: Section 138 NI Act: Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of funds or stop payment.
Section 139 NI Act: Presumption in favour of holder that the cheque was received for discharge of any debt or other liability.
Reverse Onus Clause: Included in furtherance of the legislative objective of improving the credibility of negotiable instruments.
precedent_analysis: Goa Plast (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Chico Ursula D'Souza (2003): Section 138 applies even on 'stop payment' instructions.
Krishna Janardhan Bhat v. Dattatraya G. Hegde (2008): Standard of proof for defense is 'preponderance of probabilities'.
Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee (2001): Statutory presumptions are mandatory and follow the law's language.
courts_reasoning: The accused admitted that the signature on the cheque was his own, which triggers the Section 139 presumption.
The defense of 'lost blank cheque' was found inconsistent because the instructions to the bank for 'stop payment' mentioned a specific date but did not mention the loss of the cheque.
The accused failed to reply to the statutory notice, which leads to an inference toward the complainant's version's merit.
The High Court's reversal of acquittal was justified because the accused failed to raise a 'probable defense' to rebut the statutory presumption.
conclusion: The Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with the High Court's conviction order.
The appeal was disposed of, confirming the conviction and the fine of Rs. 75,000.
full_ratio: The presumption mandated by Section 139 of the NI Act indeed includes the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. This is a rebuttable presumption in the nature of a reverse onus clause, where the accused only needs to show a 'preponderance of probabilities' to raise a probable defense.
